reviews.text: I was an early Nevergrind Online alpha and beta tester. I did not start out thinking hey, let's play this game for 1,800 hours. Well... lol... even in early alpha this was a fun way to pass the ,time. I am not hardcore, also not really an RPG player; in fact, this is the first RPG I've spent any real time playing. The game was recommended to me by a friend, and the dev gave me a key, and I started playing. I got involved in the Discord community and had a lot of fun playing with people on the Discord. The game just keeps getting better - you would not BELIEVE the patch speed - fast and responsive - and I just generally liked the stuff you do. You can play with lots of different characters, try different weapons, work on your outfit (which provides both protection and powers). The game starts in a town where you can talk to other players and group up. Honestly, that happened in the Discord but sometimes you find someone just kicking around who wants to play. There are also guilds, but in the alpha/beta there's just a core group of people so I figure that will become more important later, guild chat and all kinds of stuff I didn't use. So anyway, you pick from a list of dungeons. These start out easy - thank God because I sucked at it the first few rounds. This is not a hold your hand kind of game, but it does let you get used to things before drenching you in new scary gameplay. There are 4 phases, tougher each time, with a big scary mean dragon to defeat at the end after you beat all the other big bosses. I now have 3 level 50 characters who are CHAMPIONS. That's the top tier. My other characters are ones I get to try out, and in all these hours I still haven't really explored all the possibilities. I made a few guides for the dungeons, and helped out a bit with the wiki, but Trench did the heaviest lifting there. Go look at the wiki. If you like RPGs, blobbers (yes, I just learned what that is), dungeon crawlers, this game is great. I'm not an analytical person like some of my gaming buddies (who rock, I'm talking to you Lemmeron and Trench and Foodo). But I found a lot to love about this game. I can't wait to pay for this game. Twenty bucks is a pittance for the hours I have already spent exploring here. BTW one of my favorite characters is Druid, which has the FLAMING MEATBALL (not called that but I forget the real name now) and lots of other skills that made me laugh and have fun kicking monster butt. Hope you will enjoy it, too! 11/24/22 - Just updated hours played and wanted to add kudos to the dev for making great progress on the roadmap. The game's on sale right now for the first time! I'm still playing pretty regularly. Hope to see you in town. :) 4/7/23 - I am still playing. Still not what anyone would call hardcore though. You know how it is with games. You start, you stop, ebb, flow etc. It's so nice to be able to do that and not feel like I'm lost when I come back to play. The recent patch for joining a crew in progress of clearing a dungeon from town is a great addition! I appreciate the ongoing support of the game, and the steady work on the task list. Very professional. 11/22/23 - I hit level 95 with my main last week! I still recommend this game highly, and play when I can (who knows, maybe I'll hit 99 someday). It's nice that I can fit in gameplay here and there without losing anything - just jump right back in and go beat some monster behind. Talents are done so I will probably start some new characters and play around with other features. What a long way this game has come! Gratz to the dev and community. Game's on sale again - really happy to see a bunch of new players. :)

I'll preface this by saying -- the game has a ton of potential. If I could have given a neutral review, I would have done so. The core gameplay loop is fun. Joe did a great job of borrowing and learning from concepts from a variety of games (especially EverQuest and Diablo II). It's a good early access game. But it absolutely isn't a full game. And I do not think it will be soon. The reason that I wouldn't recommend it is because there's no endgame and (for reasons I'll describe below) I think that it's unlikely that there will be one soon. So, you can get to level 50 and then... start a new character and get to level 50 again. And because of the lack of an endgame, player retention is going to quickly become a big problem. It's really unfortunate because, with a little focus in the correct direction, I think that he could quickly build an additional content loop to retain the most dedicated players and make the leveling experience better for new players. Problems: - No character specialization: Every warrior is the same; every cleric is the same; there are no talents, no alternate advancement. The only progression is through items. And right now, the itemization doesn't allow for much specialization: - Shallow itemization: It's close to good. There are magics, rares, uniques, and set items. The piece that's missing is that the unique and set items aren't distinct enough to allow meaningful build differentiation. There's no "lightning sorc" or "frozen orb sorc". There should be unique and set items which are build enabling and build defining, but, right now they're just rare items with more consistent stats. Adding these chase uniques / sets for each class is going to be a problem, because there are too many classes. - Too many classes: Joe has done a great job of creating 14 distinct, fun classes. Each of them feels different and fun, which is no easy feat. But, there are 14 of them. And 14 classes means creating 14 talent trees. And balancing 14 talent trees. And creating meaningful itemization for 14 classes. And so on, and so on. Every additional class adds an enormous cost in terms of ongoing development and maintenance. The decision to have so many classes is going to be a permanent drag on the ability to meaningfully change the game. Is there any hope? Absolutely, yes! I'm actually pretty optimistic that in around 2 years this will be a really fully featured game. Unfortunately, though, I think that by then everyone (other than Lyra) will have quit playing. The best thing to do would be to focus effort *right now* on a simple, cross-cutting meta progression system to keep the most dedicated players engaged. There are several people who have multiple level 50 characters already. They should be given an avenue to progress their main character rather than being forced into alts. One example system would be a prestige system. Give people the option after defeating The Final Boss to be reborn as a naked level 1, but, with a persistent bonus to {gold find / magic find / whatever} and with a higher experience cost per level. Make this prestige level show up on the leaderboard. A system like this would be trivial to build, allow people an infinite grind, and also have the benefit of constantly refreshing the population of low level characters for people to play with. I really hope that I can revisit soon and flip this review to positive -- the game is close!

There are hundreds of free mobile games that are basically identical to this game, minus the multiplayer. Plus the multiplayer is kinda just annoying, and there is no option to use a NPC party, so you are forced to beg people to party up, I can imagine this game basically becoming unplayable once the hype dies down and the playerbase dies off. Why no auto combat? That's one thing mobile games of the same type do right, they have auto combat, but in this you have to manually click everything, and it becomes repetitive and boring, a simple right click to auto cast each spell would be nice. Sure I could set a macro to spam 1-= I guess, but it wouldn't be ideal, wouldn't target the right enemies or heal correctly etc. Also what's with the price? Like I said there are FREE mobile games that are fundamentally identical. If it was like 1990 I would rate this like 8/10, but in 2022 this is like 2/10 That said, it does hit a sweet spot of nostalgia, and I guess that's where the positive reviews come from. If it was like $5 I'd give it a positive review but for $30 Aussie bucks its a no buy from me.

If there was anything between yes or no for a score i'd give it that, but there isn't one and I honestly wouldn't recommend this game to anyone right now. It's missing a bunch of a basic features/QoL that really hurt the experience and skill balance isn't great. If your interest in the game isn't fueled solely by nostalgia for this kind of game, let this one bake in the oven for a while. Some thoughts: -Dev's stance on no microtransactions is rare and refreshing to see. -Solid gameplay loop. -Classes don't feel great until you get all the skills, then they stagnate because there's nothing to do other than level the skills upwards. No specialization, talent, or racial skill trees to work on to make a unique build. -Gear doesn't do much to build a certain play style & the sets I found weren't anything interesting. -Partying is fun until people get bugs and have to restart. Can't see buffs on your allies or buff timers. -LFG/LFM is cool until you realize the player pop isn't really strong enough to maintain quick or reliable grouping. -Playing solo is going to be extremely difficult for many classes, even at the basic difficulty. -The players I met in game were really chill, nice community. -There's a decent amount of portraits, but most look too similar and others don't fit the artstyle. -I don't know about the drama surrounding the dev's opinions since it was all removed from youtube, but what others have said doesn't mean much to me since I wasn't able to watch make my own opinion on them.

This game is like an old friend from the past who you just don’t want to hang out with anymore. You’ve grown up. You’re married. Maybe you even have children. Your old friend doesn’t know about these things, in fact these issues aren’t even on his radar. It’s been 10 years since you last spoke with him, but he just randomly showed up on your doorstep with a case of beer and wants nothing else but to talk about all the great times you guys had back in high school. You’ve since moved on. I have to admit it took the developers a lot of gumption to release this game in 2022. This isn’t WOW, this isn’t even EverQuest. There is no world to explore, no sense of discovery, no sights to see, no communities due to geography/faction, no crafting, no pvp, no story, etc. This is a throwback, it’s a straight up MUD with a graphical user interface slapped on top and nothing more. If that’s your thing, go ahead and enjoy this game, please don’t let a naysayer like me ruin your fun. I understand what the developers were trying to do, I actually think it's cool they even attempted to make something like this nowadays. However, if I’m being completely honest I just can’t recommend the game. I tried to like it but I simply just can't enjoy it, I've since moved on.

This game is World of Warcraft or Everquest Lite. Mechanically, combat is tab targeted, debuff/dot maintenance, cast channel bars delayed by damage (even though there's no range/roots to get uninterrupted casts, so most classes kinda suck solo)... It's all 100% exactly like those 1st generation MMOs. There's a darkest dungeon style town + procedural dungeon map and exploration instead of open world. The 14 classes are almost 1:1 with WoW; warrior/rogue/druid/shaman/monk/warlock, and slight renames like shadowknight or crusader, etc. They have the same core mechanics, too - warriors maintain bleed stacks and have big defensive cooldowns, warlocks are DoT kings, druids are about HoTs, etc. The issue is that the mechanics FEEL 20 years old. If you played WoW daily for the last 20 years but finally dropped the game, this could fill the void for practicing your rotation (except you can't rearrange your ability bar afaik). But for everyone else? These mechanics were fine when you had to worry about making it work on your dial up modem, but honestly don't hold up in 2023 - and I was bored of them more than a decade ago. Like many, any WoW time after the first few years was a socially motivated experience, not a game mechanics motivated one. NGO is a game I already played and got all the fun out of years and years ago, long before it was made. Now it just feels.. tedious. The game definitely does what it sets out to do, and it does it pretty cleanly - I like the janky indie enemy models, the UI mostly is serviceable, and I didn't experience any bugs... it's just that it's twenty years late, and apart from a niche audience that wants nostalgia without paying one of today's most disliked gaming companies any money, I don't really think there's anyone I'd actively recommend this game for.

I am a 45 yo father, probably one of the oldest people playing this game. I am a single father to my Son, who is 14 now. My son got this game for Passover in 2022 from his uncle, so we installed it on his computer and he started playing. By the end of the week he had 24 hours on this game. This was horrible for me, as it was already hard for me to find ways to spend time with my son, as he is always out with his friends or just watching YouTube. So i decided to make a Steam account and get this game to see if I could maybe play alongside him. I loaded into the game, picked my character and world and started playing but I was stuck on what you where supposed to do. I asked my Son for help and he hosted a game for me to join. I loved it as it was the best time I had spent with my Son since my wife had died. This game has ever since brought me and my son closer again and now we actually spend time together outside the house together as well. This game reminded me that there's fun to be had in everything, and it has brought both me and my Son many happy memories.

$5 Steam Sale so I grabbed it. Couple weeks and 100 hours puts me in a good place to leave a review. Cool Devs who are often online and constantly tweaking this labor of love the call NeverGrind. After a week you will be in the 90s with your 6 piece (if you have cool friends who share gear) and then you wonder what you are still doing here. A projected 1,000+ hours to get to level 100 all the while your build, skills, rotations will never change. The epileptic seizure visuals of flashing lights was nifty at first but you will find yourself looking away more often than staring at your screen. With the Devs listening to suggesting I suppose this unpolished gem could shine brightly one day. It has been promised to never be pay to win or have a cash shop so thats atleast something... Was $5 worth 100 hours of entertainment? Meh...I would rather have my time back me thinks. I could see a freemium with banner adds netting this company more money than the current business model.

[h1]Met a game online, it asked me if we wanted to be together and I said yes...[/h1] So yeah this July out of nowhere I got smacked by my gaming surprise drop of the year called Nevergrind Online and I really, [b]really[/b] love the game. It's a classic take on simple game design sporting vintage visuals. Pure nostalgia for people who played browser games of the late 90s early 2k years era, hits you like a flower power van to the face. It's addicting in terms of raw grinding experience nonstop and searching for just the right loot drops, it offers the player a lot of freedom to customize their character build (for better or for worse), all the different classes are fun and well designed. [h3]...but, I still can't recommend you playing Nevergrind Online.[/h3] And I promise this is not one of those [i]"a dude purchased a game for under 15 bucks, played almost 400 hours and gave it a negative Steam review"[/i] memes. There are two nearly insummountable issues with this game that make it not worth your time playing: [u][b]Number one: There aren't enough players.[/b][/u] This is mainly an online game, there also is a offline mode but the game is boring on your own and you can just feel it was designed with teamplay in mind. The first two weeks after 1.0 launch there were around 600 people online and it was fine. But now, come September, the average number of players online at the same time has been below 100 for quite a while. This leads to exactly what you'd expect: Maybe two full parties going on for endgame and a few low to mid level players running around, with some people being afk in town. It has gotten really difficult to get things going. Now imagine ten people are in two parties and the eleventh guy comes online - they got nowhere to go but play on their own, and that is a constant issue. The problem has also been made worse by the fact that many of the biggest fans are now multiboxing for tripple the loot and don't even team up with others anymore. In addition to that there is an established powerlevel culture, because once you've done it once the lower to mid levels are terribly boring to play and most people wish to skip it. Which is understandable but doesn't work with potential new players (aka you, the reader) who first have to slowly learn the game. There are not just cons to this, for example the playerbase consists mostly of older people of whom the majority are either very friendly and polite, or at least not impolite. New players can expect a lot of advice, help and free gear because everyone's bank is stacked up with items at this point. But again the low player numbers make it so there is basically no item market because no one needs anything except the really rare best in slot or very specific talent rolls items, so stuff is just sitting in the bank for the next alt character or without real use at all. And because so few people are creating items from their loot, the top dogs in the player pool can offer tens of millions in gold for a single piece and still not have anybody sell it to them, simply because the wanted combination has never been found. It's just a pretty sad and hopeless feeling all around when the game feels insufficently frequented by other players. [u][b]Number two: A single dev can't run an online game.[/b][/u] I don't want to bash on the guy, he did an admirable job programming this game, putting it online, keeping people engaged in the Discord - but it's simply a task too large for one person, or even a team of several volunteers. There were painful issues with group finding for a really long time, because 1.0 launched in a not quite ready state and met more people than expected. I don't even want to go into detail how many different bugs can occur while you simply want to join up with others, but I will say despite other claims not all of them have been fixed. This cost a lot of players who simply lost patience. When you offer an online coop multiplayer game, your number one top priority should be getting people into games with another as smoothly and hazzle free as possible - but the opposite is true for Nevergrind. And then, what the one person bringing this game to us does not have is consultants: Voices of reason. He's a stubborn one, has to be to make a game like this. But this leads to other issues: One time the guy decided he wanted to change the group finder to not display all parties anymore, but only those that you could actually join (has a free spot, got difficulty unlocked, and you meet their requirenments) for better visibility. But what really happend from this change is the group finder looks like the empty wasteland of a dead game. People look at it and say omg no party, wait in town because they don't want to start a group themselves and do the walking part. Dev never took that change back despite the obvious consequences and it literally caused the largest player drop just from this. Another time the dev decided to change some damaging mechanics, then spent three days correcting the mistakes over and over again because it was not tested and overtuned. That time would have been better spent on fixing online connection stability or getting us closer to new content. And stuff like that happens on a regular basis. When there is only one person looking at the workload it's easy to become lost. There is a deeply rooted structural problem that causes this game to be stuck in place. [h3]Anyway, if you've made it this far and still think about playing the game because nothing can scare you away, hop right in we'd love to have ya![/h3]

TLDR: This is an independent project - so while I am harsh on it - I appreciate and respect the work involved! I wouldn't ask for my time back, and I would be glad to play with a full group of buddies -- but I would NOT recommend spending your money on it in the current state of the game. The game is called Nevergrind Online - so they immediately start with a lie. The game is 110% grind. The name also ends with a lie - in implying there will ever be that many people online. When the game was first ported to steam - the servers were lively and busy! Then Covid passed and people could go outside and do things - leaving a few time-to-time players, diehards, and tourists. I've logged in during what I would assume to be peak hours (friday nights, weekends) to see only one or two incomplete parties running dungeons. The talent 'trees' lack 'choice' - they're just raw upgrades down three paths. Each tree roughly covers a third of your abilities and augments them (the first half are usually base stat increases, the second half usually modify the effects somehow). So - what remains in the game is a lootfest. Min-max your stats, run dungeons, rinse repeat. I had fun with it - but the community is nonexistent.

NGO currently has a 1-week peak of 66 players online. Finding lobbies with players who are your level to play with is effectively not possible, and you're basically relegated to only playing this game singleplayer. This works for some fighter/DPS classes, but this is a party-based blobber; There's no use for tanks or healers, which are 2/3 of the roaster, if you only play this singleplayer... and then there's almost no challenge whatsoever without multiplayer scaling. There's really exactly like this concept on the market, which sucks because I thought this game was pretty cool on release.
